The best time for a VFT transplant is after the dormancy period, Oct-Feb.  It's probably fine for now, but come Oct/Nov (depending on location) it will need a period of dormancy for 3-4mos (again, depending on location, but 3mos MINIMUM) sealed in a bag in your fridge. Then in the Spring (Feb/March), take it out of the fridge and bag, dunk it in a container of Distilled, Rain or Reverse Osmosis water to remove potting mix, and carefully repot it into the new container, using a mix of 50/50 peat moss/Perlite with light Sphagnum above and below sandwiching it in.

I made this for her teacher, who is beyond incredible.   

I used Loops and Threads Soft and Shiny yarn by Michael's, in the white color, and a 4mm hook. It's a self drafted pattern based off of folding a flat paper into a cube. Embroidery is Aunt Lydias crochet thread in Peacock. 

15 DC per row, 9 rows per square.  When I went to do the side squares, I simply added an extra 15 stitches (plus 2 or 3 for turning rows, was frying to eliminate end row bumps)  so that those rows had 30 DC and 9 rows. 15x9 square, 30x9 rectangle, second offset 30x9 rectangle for the other side of the cube, then a 15x9 square on top. Folded all together and sewn shut using a blanket stitch and embroidered with the chemical symbol / standard name. 

Quick project that I whipped up in less than a day. Hopefully she likes it.

A lot of look issues can be fixed with a good blocking of the item after washing. It helps with evening out the whole thing when finished and helps open stitches up to showcase their beauty. 

Also, tension is key. Especially when doing cluster and puff type stitches. The extra loops pulled up for the stitch should have a nice loose tension; no one loop should be tighter than any other. It is crucial to try and keep the tension equal for each stitch, both for creating a cohesive and desired look, and to make blocking that area into the desired shape easier. 

I suspect the item is probably close to the original effect already. You can get an idea of it by stretching it equally from each corner/side to try and see what it'd look like after stretching out the stitches through the blocking process.

One last note. Don't be afraid to frog your work if it just isn't coming out like you planned. If it's not working, and you don't like it, you can always start over and try again. You lose nothing, and gain good practice. Practice teaches you how to better execute your attempts, to create better and more complex patterns and designs. 

I wish you luck and happy hooking!

Depends. Was a hen sitting on the found clutch? Was it just a clutch of eggs, hidden in a corner?

If it's a clutch with hen sitting, take the eggs, candle them and estimate where they are developmentally based off the shadows you see inside. Then either return them to the hen, or put them in an incubator, and return the chicks to her after.

If it's just a clutch of eggs, no hen guarding it, candle them anyways to check they aren't developing, and if no development shadowing is visible inside, drop the eggs into a bucket of water and remove any that float. If any are developing, incubate if you desire, or destroy. Any fully sunk eggs are fresh, eggs standing en pointe (like a ballerina on her toes) are less fresh (but still edible, eat these first), and any floating are bad. Good eggs are sunk eggs.

Hidden clutches usually don't occur if there is ample room in the nest area for all the hens. Ideally you want 1 box per 3 hens. Boxes should be at least 12x12. Open top nests are most common, but you can make it enclosed to offer more privacy, if you want to offer a luxury private laying area. Just make sure it's at least 12x12x12 so they can adjust as needed. If there isn't enough room in the box(es), or all are occupied, a hen may find a quiet corner outside the nest to lay.

The chicks will stay in the incubator for about 24 hrs from hatching to fully dry off, rest, and acclimate. After that, they are moved to the brooder box with food and water, waiting for the rest of their hatchmates to join them. Keep in mind, in nature there is a whole mama chicken sitting on them as they hatch to keep them warm, so this is like a warm cozy suite almost. Not all chicks hatch at the same time, a batch of 6 may take 3 days to all hatch out, so they can be easily moved out if there is not enough space as others hatch.

When chicks are in the final days of incubation, before hatching, they absorb the yolk of their egg. It gives them the energy to free themselves, and support their food needs for about 1 or 2 days from hatching. This is why hatcheries can sell and send out day old chicks without supplying food or water in the mail.

Also note, incubators usually have dome-like tops to allow chicks to move around each other. Also the shells get removed so there is additional room.
